content.title: About
content.content: Chewing gum is a sweet or flavored rubbery mass designed for chewing. It typically consists of a gum base, sweeteners, flavorings, and sometimes softening agents. Chewing gum is not intended to be swallowed.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first modern chewing gum was invented by William S. White in 1869.
In the 1970s, chewing gum was used in space missions to help astronauts relieve stress.
Sugar‑free gum contains sweetener substitutes such as xylitol, which is beneficial for teeth.
Chewing gum can improve concentration and memory by increasing blood flow to the brain.
In some countries chewing gum is banned in schools due to the risk of it being swallowed.

items.title: Stimulates saliva production
items.content: Chewing increases saliva flow, which helps neutralize acids and reduces the risk of cavities.

items.title: Improves focus
items.content: Studies show that chewing can boost attention and short‑term memory.

items.title: Reduces stress
items.content: The mechanical act of chewing promotes relaxation and lowers cortisol levels.

items.title: Supports oral hygiene
items.content: Sugar‑free varieties with xylitol can inhibit the growth of cavity‑causing bacteria.

items.title: Aids smoking cessation
items.content: Chewing gum is often used as a nicotine replacement to curb cravings.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to flavorings, sweeteners, or the gum base.

items.title: Gastrointestinal discomfort
items.content: Excessive chewing can cause stomach upset, gas, or heartburn.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Small pieces of gum can be dangerous for young children if swallowed.

items.title: Sweetener concerns
items.content: Sugar‑containing gum can promote cavities, while some sugar substitutes (e.g., sorbitol) may cause diarrhea in large amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chew the gum slowly without swallowing. Sugar‑free versions are recommended after meals to improve oral hygiene. Avoid chewing for more than 15‑20 minutes at a time.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store gum in a cool, dry place in a tightly sealed package to prevent drying out and loss of flavor. For long‑term storage, keep it in the refrigerator.

content.title: About
content.content: Liquid coffee creamer is a ready‑to‑use beverage additive that gives coffee a creamy taste and smoother texture. It usually contains dairy or plant‑based fats, sweeteners, flavorings, and stabilizers that keep it homogeneous when mixed with hot coffee.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial creamer appeared in the United States in the 1950s as an alternative to fresh cream.
Creamers are often used in decaffeinated and flavored drinks to enhance their flavor profile.
Most liquid creamers dissolve instantly in hot coffee without the need for whisking.
There are lactose‑free and plant‑based versions suitable for vegans and those with dairy intolerance.
Emulsifiers such as lecithin are added to prevent separation.

items.title: Improves coffee taste
items.content: The creamy aroma and smooth texture make coffee more enjoyable, especially for those who dislike bitterness.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Some creamers are fortified with riboflavin (B2) and cobalamin (B12), which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Provides quick energy
items.content: Fats and carbohydrates supply a fast source of calories, useful in the morning.

items.title: Enhances satiety
items.content: The fat content can slow caffeine absorption, giving a more gradual stimulant effect.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Dairy‑based creamers may trigger reactions in people allergic to casein.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Sweetened versions can raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: Some products use partially hydrogenated oils that contain trans fats, which are harmful to heart health.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Liquid creamers are relatively calorie‑dense, so they should be used in moderation.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add 10–30 ml of creamer to hot coffee and stir. It works well in lattes, cappuccinos, mochas, and cold coffee drinks. For diet‑friendly options choose sugar‑free or plant‑based creamers.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the creamer in the refrigerator at 1 °C–4 °C. After opening, use within 7–10 days. Do not freeze, as this may alter the texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Pozole is a traditional Mexican soup made from hominy (alkaline‑treated corn kernels), meat (usually pork) and aromatic spices. The dish has a thick, stew‑like consistency and a smoky flavor derived from chipotle, dried chilies and herbs.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pozole uses nixtamalized corn, which is soaked in an alkaline solution before cooking.
The dish dates back over 500 years to the Aztec civilization, where it was prepared for ritual purposes.
There are two main styles: red pozole (with chipotle) and green pozole (with tomatillo and green chilies).
Pozole is commonly served on holidays such as Día de los Muertos and at family gatherings.
In Mexico, pozole is considered a comfort food that warms you on cold days.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Hominy provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: The combination of meat and corn delivers a complete set of essential amino acids.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Pozole contains thiamine, niacin and vitamin B6, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The soup supplies iron, magnesium and zinc, important for blood health and immunity.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Chipotle and dried chilies are rich in carotenoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Traditional broth can be salty; people with hypertension should watch their salt intake.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to corn, leading to allergic reactions.

items.title: Fatty meat
items.content: Pork can be fatty; lean cuts or chicken can be used as a lighter alternative.

items.title: Spicy chilies
items.content: Chili peppers may irritate the stomach of those with gastritis or ulcers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve pozole hot, topped with lime wedges, sliced avocado, fresh cilantro, radishes and tortilla strips. Optional additions include sour cream or crumbled queso fresco.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. When frozen, pozole retains quality for about 2 months; thaw in the fridge before reheating.
